nameStory: Holmes' hawthorn is named after a botanist who helped identify and describe this particular species. Like all hawthorns, it gets its common name from the Old English 'haegthorn,' meaning 'hedge thorn' - a nod to their traditional use as living fences that could keep livestock penned in with their fierce thorns.
description: Holmes' hawthorn is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that belongs to the rose family, sharing kinship with apples, cherries, and roses. Like its hawthorn cousins, it produces clusters of small white flowers in spring followed by small red fruits called haws. It typically grows 15-25 feet tall with a rounded crown and armed branches that bear sharp thorns. This is an extremely rare species in New England, with only a handful of documented sightings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are more elongated than typical hawthorns, with a somewhat oval shape and serrated edges that feel slightly rough to the touch. They're arranged alternately on branches and turn various shades of orange to red in fall.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small red berries (haws) are noticeably more elongated and egg-shaped compared to the rounder fruits of most hawthorns. They ripen in late summer and often persist into winter, feeling firm when fresh.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Clusters of small white flowers appear in late spring, each with five petals and a sweet, somewhat musky fragrance. The flower clusters are showy against the fresh green leaves.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray-brown bark becomes scaly and furrowed with age. Young branches are smooth and reddish-brown, while older trunks develop a rough, plated texture you can feel with your fingers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a small tree or large shrub with a rounded crown and somewhat irregular branching pattern. Sharp thorns, up to 2 inches long, project from branches and can easily snag clothing.

habitat: Holmes' hawthorn is found in woodland edges, old fields, and disturbed areas with well-drained soils. It tolerates various soil types but seems to prefer slightly acidic conditions typical of New England's forests. Given its rarity, specific habitat preferences in New England are not well documented.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters bloom in May, creating showy displays that attract bees and other pollinators. New leaves emerge bright green with a fresh, slightly fuzzy texture.
seasonality.summer: Leaves are fully developed and deep green. Small green fruits begin forming and gradually enlarge throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn orange to reddish colors before dropping. The elongated red fruits ripen and become prominent, often persisting after leaf fall.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the thorny structure and scaly bark pattern. Persistent red fruits may remain visible into early winter, and sharp thorns are easily felt.

funFact: Holmes' hawthorn is so rare in New England that it has been documented only three times - making it more elusive than some orchids and about as likely to spot as finding a needle in a haystack!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with scarlet hawthorn, but Holmes' hawthorn has distinctly more elongated leaves and egg-shaped fruits rather than the rounder features of scarlet hawthorn. Remember: 'Holmes has longer bones' - both the leaves and fruits are more stretched out.
contextualKnowledge: Hawthorn identification is notoriously difficult even for botanists, as the genus contains dozens of species that can hybridize and show variable characteristics. Many hawthorn species were named after the botanists who first described them, leading to a confusing array of names that don't reflect the plants' actual appearance.
compareHints: Holmes' hawthorn is most closely related to scarlet hawthorn but distinguished by its more elongated leaves and egg-shaped rather than round fruits. Compared to the more common dotted hawthorn found in New England, Holmes' hawthorn lacks the distinctive dotted fruit surface and has different leaf proportions. The elongated features of both leaves and fruits are the key distinguishing characteristics from other regional hawthorns.

Among New England's many hawthorn species, cockspur stands out with the longest thorns - much longer than dotted hawthorn's short spines or Washington hawthorn's modest thorns.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, big-fruit hawthorn stands out for its notably larger berries and earlier bloom time.
Among New England hawthorns, large-thorn hawthorn stands out primarily for its exceptionally long, straight thorns that dwarf those of relatives like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn.

Among the many hawthorn species in New England, Washington hawthorn stands out with its distinctly triangular, deeply lobed leaves (rather than the more oval or rounded leaves of species like dotted hawthorn).
Among New England's many hawthorn species, waxy-fruited hawthorn stands out primarily for its distinctively coated berries - no other local hawthorn has that waxy, frosted appearance on the fruits.

Among New England's many hawthorns, downy hawthorn stands out for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - most others like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have smooth or only slightly hairy leaves.
Blanchard's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having more deeply lobed leaves and longer thorns.

Fleshy hawthorn stands out from its many hawthorn relatives by having the juiciest, most succulent berries in the group.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, scarlet hawthorn is distinguished by its particularly prominent thorns and bright red fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, Schuette's hawthorn is distinguished by subtle characteristics that require expert identification.
Northern hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less deeply lobed leaves and different fruit characteristics, though these distinctions can be subtle.
Dodge's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less prominently marked leaves and typically fewer, larger thorns.

Grove hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having longer thorns and less deeply cut leaves.

Among New England hawthorns, poplar hawthorn stands out immediately for its broad, oval, relatively unlobed leaves - most other hawthorns like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have deeply cut, lobed leaves.
